title: Benchmarks: published figures on young people, work and health-related benefits
note: Reference figures from the review (From a Welfare State to a Working State, 17 November 2026) and other sources, as published, each with its own definitions, coverage and date. Where PolicyEngine has a figure on the same basis (the same ages, area, year and measure), it is shown beside the published one with its build and year; the review's own estimates, which include replacement awards and employment effects, are shown without one.

rows.figure: Young people aged 16 to 24 not in education, employment or training (NEET)
rows.basis: Labour Force Survey estimate, April to June 2026, UK: 13.0% of people aged 16 to 24. The review describes the number as nearly one million young people, 1 in 8
rows.source: Office for National Statistics

rows.figure: NEET rate the review projects for 2036-37 with its recommendations
rows.basis: Share of people aged 16 to 24 not in education, employment or training, UK, from 13.1% in 2026-27: the review's internal modelling (data tables, table 3). The review's ambition is around 5% (paragraph 142)
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State: data tables

rows.figure: Young people on Universal Credit health with no work requirements
rows.basis: Basis not published: the Resolution Foundation gives no age range, date or source. Its own count four days later, people aged 16 to 24 receiving the health element, is a third lower (176,000). The nearest official count, DWP's Universal Credit claimants aged 16 to 24 with no work requirements in Great Britain, averaged 294,566 in 2025 and covers every reason, not only health
rows.source: Resolution Foundation

rows.figure: Young people aged 16 to 24 receiving the Universal Credit health element
rows.basis: Resolution Foundation response to the review: people aged 16 to 24 currently receiving the health element of Universal Credit
rows.source: Resolution Foundation

policyengine_estimate.basis: People aged 16 to 24 receiving the Universal Credit health element, Great Britain, 2025 (2025-26 rules), at the build's calibrated weights
policyengine_estimate.label: PolicyEngine, build fcfac709, 2025
policyengine_estimate.note: Why ours is higher: the data's UC take-up draw adds claimants who carry the element where they receive PIP, so the build counts about a third more young recipients than published

rows.figure: Share of 16 to 24-year-olds receiving the Universal Credit health element who also receive PIP
rows.basis: Resolution Foundation response to the review: 110,000 of the 176,000 people aged 16 to 24 receiving the health element of Universal Credit also receive PIP. It gives no source, date or area for the counts
rows.source: Resolution Foundation

policyengine_estimate.basis: People aged 16 to 24 receiving the Universal Credit health element who also receive PIP, Great Britain, 2025 (2025-26 rules), at the build's calibrated weights
policyengine_estimate.label: PolicyEngine, build fcfac709, 2025
policyengine_estimate.note: The overlap affects how many young people would lose both payments under the package. Our data's UC take-up draw adds health element claimants among PIP recipients, which raises the overlap

rows.figure: Young people receiving incapacity benefits, as stated in the review
rows.basis: The review's own count (paragraph 633): more than double the number in 2012
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State

rows.figure: Young people receiving Personal Independence Payment (PIP)
rows.value: 450,000; worth around £8,400 a year on average
rows.basis: Resolution Foundation response to the review: young people currently receiving PIP
rows.source: Resolution Foundation

policyengine_estimate.basis: People aged 16 to 24 receiving PIP, England and Wales, 2025, at the build's calibrated weights. DWP's 2025 count for the same group is 407,505 (England 384,150, Wales 23,355)
policyengine_estimate.label: PolicyEngine, build fcfac709, 2025
policyengine_estimate.note: DWP's 2025 count for the same ages and area: 407,505. The published 450,000 is current (November 2026), so it includes the caseload's growth since 2025

rows.figure: Young people aged 16 to 24 receiving Disability Living Allowance or PIP, as stated in the review
rows.value: Over 400,000; 820,000 expected to receive PIP in ten years
rows.basis: The review's own count from DWP Stat-Xplore (paragraph 633): double the number in 2012. The projection is 1 in 9 young people in the UK
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State

rows.figure: Young people the review expects its recommendations to help into sustained work by 2036
rows.basis: Modelling carried out for the review: the whole set of recommendations, not the benefit changes alone
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State

rows.figure: Young people affected by the modelled package
rows.basis: No published figure: shown for the PolicyEngine estimate only

policyengine_estimate.label: People aged 16 to 24 in households made worse off by the combined package
policyengine_estimate.note: Our data put 90.6% of 16 to 24-year-olds receiving the UC health element on PIP too, against 62.5% in the Resolution Foundation's figures, so more of these young people lose both payments in our data than the published counts imply

rows.figure: Spending on PIP and Universal Credit health for young people
rows.value: £4.7bn a year; £1.7bn in 2019-20, forecast at £8.8bn in 2036-37
rows.basis: The review's figures for ages 16 to 24 in 2025-26 (paragraph 114): PIP of £3.8bn and the Universal Credit LCWRA element of £0.92bn
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State

policyengine_estimate.basis: Spending in 2025 (2025-26 rules), cash terms: PIP at ages 16 to 24 in England and Wales (£3.27bn) and the Universal Credit health element for young claimants in Great Britain (£1.18bn)
policyengine_estimate.label: PolicyEngine, build fcfac709, 2025, cash terms
policyengine_estimate.note: Close because two gaps offset: PIP is 14% lower than the review's figure and the health element 28% higher

policyengine_saving.label: Our saving from removing them, 2029-30, cash terms
policyengine_saving.basis: Static Exchequer saving in 2029-30 from removing the UC health element for under-25s and PIP for ages 18 to 24, UK, cash terms, including knock-on effects on other benefits, all within Universal Credit in the model (such as the disabled child element, entitlement while in education and the housing element's shared accommodation rate; Carer's Allowance does not change in the model): a saving, not spending; PIP at 16 and 17 is not removed

rows.figure: PIP spending on people aged 16 to 24
rows.value: £3.8bn a year; £1.3bn in 2019-20, forecast at £8.1bn in 2036-37
rows.basis: The review's figure for 2025-26, ages 16 to 24 (footnote to paragraph 114)
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State

policyengine_estimate.basis: PIP spending on people aged 16 to 24, England and Wales, 2025 (2025-26 rules), cash terms
policyengine_estimate.label: PolicyEngine, build fcfac709, 2025, cash terms
policyengine_estimate.note: Why ours is lower: the caseload matches DWP's 2025 count, but the review's figure is for the 2025-26 financial year and the build's average award is lower (about £8,000 a year, against the Resolution Foundation's £8,400)

policyengine_saving.label: Our saving from removing PIP at 16 to 24, 2029-30, cash terms
policyengine_saving.basis: Static Exchequer saving from removing PIP for ages 16 to 24 in 2029-30, UK, cash terms, including knock-on effects on other benefits, all within Universal Credit in the model (such as the disabled child element, entitlement while in education and the housing element's shared accommodation rate; Carer's Allowance does not change in the model), so not the same as PIP spending; £3.64bn for ages 18 to 24

rows.figure: Universal Credit LCWRA element spending on people aged 16 to 24
rows.value: £0.92bn a year; £0.42bn in 2019-20, forecast at £0.68bn in 2036-37
rows.basis: The review's figure for 2025-26, ages 16 to 24 (footnote to paragraph 114)
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State

policyengine_estimate.basis: Universal Credit health element spending on young claimants, Great Britain, 2025 (2025-26 rules), cash terms
policyengine_estimate.label: PolicyEngine, build fcfac709, 2025, cash terms
policyengine_estimate.note: Why ours is higher: the same excess as in the caseload, where the build has about a third more young people receiving the element than published counts

policyengine_saving.label: Our saving from removing it for under-25s, 2029-30, cash terms
policyengine_saving.basis: Static Exchequer saving from removing the UC health element for under-25s in 2029-30, UK, cash terms

rows.figure: Annual welfare saving the review estimates for 2036-37
rows.basis: PIP and Universal Credit spending, UK, in 2026-27 prices, against the baseline forecast: replacement awards for some claimants, the cost of a Youth Allowance and a work allowance, and an assumed employment effect. Savings begin in 2029-30
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State: analytical annex

rows.figure: Cumulative welfare savings the review estimates by 2036-37
rows.basis: Sum of annual savings over the eight years from 2029-30 to 2036-37, UK, in 2026-27 prices (paragraph 113 and the analytical annex)
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State

rows.figure: Annual cost of the review's recommendations in 2036-37
rows.value: £5.8bn in 2036-37; a net saving of about £0.2bn after welfare savings and fiscal offsets
rows.basis: Gross cost in 2026-27 prices (data tables, table 2): education £2.1bn, Opportunity and Support Guarantees £1.9bn, youth hiring incentives £1.1bn, health £0.7bn; set against £3.6bn of welfare savings and £2.4bn of fiscal offsets
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State: data tables

rows.figure: Cost of the review's youth hiring incentives in 2036-37
rows.basis: Gross cost in 2026-27 prices of expanding the Youth Jobs Grant by up to 40,000 places a year and of the apprenticeship recommendations. The annex gives no separate cost for the employer National Insurance change the review proposes
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State: analytical annex

rows.figure: Incapacity benefit spending on people aged 18 to 24
rows.basis: IFS analysis
rows.source: Institute for Fiscal Studies

rows.figure: Cost of a zero employer National Insurance rate for under-25s
rows.value: £5.1bn a year; about £132,000 per extra job
rows.basis: Resolution Foundation estimate (Take a chance on me, 29 June 2026, Figure 10, as corrected on 2 September): the gross fiscal cost in 2025-26, in 2025-26 prices, of scrapping employer National Insurance for under-25s on top of the existing zero rate for under-21s, with 38,500 extra young workers. Not a recommendation of the review, which proposes a higher employer National Insurance threshold for workers aged 21 to 24 instead
rows.source: Resolution Foundation

policyengine_estimate.basis: Gross static cost in 2025-26 of a zero employer National Insurance rate for under-25s, on top of the existing zero rate for under-21s, UK, cash terms
policyengine_estimate.label: PolicyEngine, build fcfac709, 2025-26, cash terms
policyengine_estimate.note: Why ours is higher: the build has about 10% fewer payroll employees aged 18 to 24 than HMRC's count, so the difference points to pay per young employee, which is not a calibration target

policyengine_saving.label: Our net cost, 2029-30, cash terms
policyengine_saving.basis: Static cost of a zero employer National Insurance rate for under-25s in 2029-30, UK, cash terms, net of the income tax and National Insurance on the higher pay that employers' saving passes into

rows.figure: Change in relative poverty after housing costs the review estimates
rows.basis: People in relative low income after housing costs once the modelled measures are fully rolled out, to the nearest 50,000: benefit changes with replacement awards, a Health and Disability Fund, a Youth Allowance, a work allowance and 440,000 more young people in work
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State: analytical annex

rows.figure: Young people kept out of poverty by UC health and/or PIP
rows.basis: Resolution Foundation analysis
rows.source: Resolution Foundation

rows.figure: Young PIP claimants reporting no extra costs
rows.basis: Resolution Foundation research
rows.source: Resolution Foundation

rows.figure: Rise in young people's net incomes the review estimates
rows.basis: All the review's reforms considered together (paragraphs 111 and 739; analytical annex, section 7): the earnings of young people the review expects to move into work, less the modelled welfare savings and fiscal offsets. No year or price basis is given with the figure
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State

rows.figure: Share of jobs for people aged 16 to 24 in retail and hospitality, as stated in the review
rows.basis: The review's figure (paragraph 50), from the Office for National Statistics' employment by industry section and age group to 2025 (footnote 14), for retail and hospitality, which we take to be sections G (wholesale and retail trade) and I (accommodation and food service)
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State

rows.figure: PIP spending on people aged 16 to 24 over time, as stated in the review
rows.value: Around £3.2bn in 2024-25; around £1.3bn in 2019-20, around £6.5bn within five years
rows.basis: The review's figures (paragraph 653): annual PIP spending on people aged 16 to 24, around £3.2bn in 2024-25, up from around £1.3bn in 2019-20, and around £6.5bn within five years on the interim report's central trajectory
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State

rows.figure: Universal Credit spending on young people with a health issue, as stated in the review
rows.basis: The review's figure (paragraph 653): the overall spend on Universal Credit for young people with a health issue, which almost doubled between 2019-20 and 2024-25
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State

rows.figure: Hidden NEETs in England: out of work and education and not receiving benefits
rows.basis: The review's figure (paragraphs 51 and 275, from its interim report): people aged 18 to 24 in England in 2023-24 neither in work nor in education and not themselves receiving benefits. Extending the Youth Jobs Grant to them could add up to 40,000 recipients a year (paragraph 275)
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State

rows.figure: Disabled people aged 16 to 24 not in education, employment or training (NEET)
rows.basis: The review's figures for 2025-26 (paragraph 692, from its interim report and DWP's The employment of disabled people 2026): disabled young people were around 3.5 times as likely to be NEET
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State

rows.figure: Children receiving Disability Living Allowance, as stated in the review
rows.value: Over 900,000; about 77% move to PIP by 17
rows.basis: The review's figures (paragraph 759, from DWP's DLA and PIP data): children under 16 receiving child Disability Living Allowance, a number rising year on year; about 77% of claimants move onto PIP by the age of 17
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State
